key_terms.meaning: A model ŷ = w₀ + w₁x₁ + … + w_dx_d that predicts a numeric target as a weighted sum of inputs.
Pick weights w that minimise the sum of squared residuals Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)².
eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ, the signed error on one training example.
Linear model with d ≥ 1 inputs: ŷ = w₀ + w₁x₁ + … + w_dx_d, written ŷ = wᵀx with x₀ = 1.
L(w) = (1/n) Σ ℓ(yᵢ, f_w(xᵢ)), a single number that training tries to reduce.
w ← w − η ∇L(w): move each weight opposite the gradient to go downhill.
η > 0, the step size in gradient descent; too large diverges, too small is slow.
Update after one example (or a small batch): w ← w − η ∇ℓᵢ(w), cheaper per step but noisier.
σ(z) = 1/(1 + e⁻ᶻ), squashes any real score z into a probability in (0, 1).
log(p/(1−p)) = wᵀx; logistic regression is linear in log-odds, not in p.
L = −(1/n) Σ [yᵢ log pᵢ + (1−yᵢ) log(1−pᵢ)], the standard logistic-regression loss.
g_c(x) = w_cᵀx + b_c for class c; predict the class with the largest g_c(x).
Train one binary classifier per class against all others, then pick the class with the highest score.
Low training error but high test error, because the model fitted noise instead of the pattern.
E[(y − f̂(x))²] = bias² + variance + σ²; simpler models raise bias, complex ones raise variance.
Minimise RSS + λ Σ wⱼ²; shrinks weights smoothly towards zero but rarely exactly to zero.
Minimise RSS + λ Σ |wⱼ|; can set some weights exactly to zero, so it also selects features.
Split data into k folds; train on k−1 folds, test on the held-out fold, average the k errors.
A table of true versus predicted labels with counts TP, FP, FN and TN.
R² = 1 − SS_res/SS_tot, the fraction of the variance in y explained by the model.

takeaways: Least squares has a closed-form solution and is the baseline every regression model is compared against.
Gradient descent is the general training recipe: batch uses all data per step, stochastic uses one point, mini-batch sits between them.
Logistic regression is linear in log-odds, and the 0.5 probability threshold is what turns it into a classifier.
A linear classifier simply picks the class whose linear discriminant score is largest; multiclass problems become several binary scores.
Overfitting is diagnosed by the gap between training and validation error, never by low training error alone.
Bias and variance pull in opposite directions, so model complexity is chosen to balance them, not to minimise either.
Ridge shrinks all weights smoothly; lasso drives some weights to exactly zero and therefore selects features.
Cross-validation estimates test error from limited data, and the chosen metric must match the real cost of mistakes.
bank_note: Long answers here are marked for the full chain — state the loss, derive or write the update rule, then finish with a validation plan and the metric you would report.

bank.q: Define simple linear regression. Derive the least-squares estimates of the slope and intercept for one input variable, and state what each symbol means.
outline: Model ŷ = w₀ + w₁x and residual eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ
Minimise RSS = Σ(yᵢ − w₀ − w₁xᵢ)²
Set partial derivatives to zero
w₁ = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / Σ(xᵢ − x̄)², w₀ = ȳ − w₁x̄
Interpret w₁ as change in ŷ per unit change in x

bank.q: Explain gradient descent. Compare batch gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent in cost per step, smoothness of the path and convergence.
outline: Update rule w ← w − η ∇L(w)
Gradient is the direction of steepest increase; move opposite
Batch: gradient over all n points, stable, expensive per step
SGD: gradient over one point, cheap but noisy, often needs decaying η
Mini-batch as the practical compromise

bank.q: Explain logistic regression. Why is a sigmoid used, what does the log-odds form mean, and where is the decision boundary for a 0.5 threshold?
outline: Linear score z = wᵀx, probability p = σ(z)
σ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ) keeps p in (0,1)
log(p/(1−p)) = wᵀx, so weights act on log-odds
Decision boundary wᵀx = 0 for threshold 0.5
Cross-entropy loss and its gradient

bank.q: Define overfitting and underfitting, sketch the typical training and validation error curves against model complexity, and explain the bias–variance trade-off.
outline: Definitions and symptoms of each
Training error falls with complexity; validation error is U-shaped
Bias = error from wrong assumptions; variance = sensitivity to the training sample
Decomposition E[(y − f̂)²] = bias² + variance + σ²
Choose complexity at the validation minimum, then regularise

bank.q: Explain ridge and lasso regression. Give the objective functions and explain why the L1 penalty produces sparse solutions while L2 does not.
outline: Ridge: RSS + λ Σ wⱼ²; Lasso: RSS + λ Σ |wⱼ|
λ ≥ 0 controls penalty strength; λ = 0 is ordinary least squares
Geometric argument: L1 constraint diamond has corners on axes
Lasso sets some coefficients exactly to zero; ridge only shrinks
Effect on variance and on interpretability

bank.q: A dataset of house sizes x (in square feet) and prices y (in lakh rupees) gives x̄ and ȳ with Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) and Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² known. Compute the least-squares line and predict the price for a given size.
outline: Substitute into w₁ and w₀ formulas
State units of slope (lakh rupees per square foot)
Compute predicted value ŷ = w₀ + w₁x for the asked size
Mention that extrapolation far outside the data range is risky

bank.q: A logistic regression model has weights w = (w₀, w₁, w₂). Given one input point, compute the score, the probability and the predicted class at threshold 0.5, then compute its cross-entropy contribution.
outline: z = w₀ + w₁x₁ + w₂x₂
p = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ) with correct arithmetic
Class 1 if p ≥ 0.5, else 0
Loss contribution −[y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)]
Note that a confident wrong prediction costs a lot

bank.q: A 5-fold cross-validation gives fold errors 0.42, 0.51, 0.38, 0.47, 0.45. Compute the mean and standard deviation, and compare this model with a second whose mean is 0.44 but whose folds vary from 0.30 to 0.60.
outline: Mean = sum/5
Standard deviation from the five fold errors
Report both mean and spread, not just the mean
Higher variance means the estimate is less trustworthy
Tie-break rule: prefer the simpler or more stable model

bank.q: Three classes are scored by linear discriminant functions g₁(x), g₂(x), g₃(x) at a test point. Given the scores, state the predicted class, and describe how a one-vs-rest scheme would train the three functions.
outline: Predict argmax_c g_c(x)
One-vs-rest: class c positive, other two negative
Fit three binary logistic or least-squares classifiers
Compare scores at prediction time
Mention ties and class imbalance in the binary problems

bank.q: A model with 200 features fits the training set to 100% accuracy but scores 62% on held-out data. Diagnose the problem and propose a full plan using regularisation, cross-validation and a baseline.
outline: Identify overfitting from the train–test gap
Compare against a simple baseline such as logistic regression with few features
Add L2 or L1 penalty; tune λ by k-fold cross-validation
Standardise features before penalising
Report validation metric with spread; consider more data or feature selection
Check for leakage between training and validation

bank.q: Compare batch gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent and mini-batch gradient descent for a large dataset. Discuss per-iteration cost, variance of updates, effect of learning rate and a practical stopping rule.
outline: Cost per step scales with n, 1 and batch size b
Noise in SGD helps escape flat regions but needs a decaying η
Mini-batch exploits vectorised hardware
Convergence is judged on validation loss, not training loss
Early stopping and learning-rate schedules

bank.q: A bank wants to flag fraudulent UPI transactions, which are 1 in 1000. Explain why accuracy is a poor metric, build the confusion matrix, and choose between precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC for this task.
outline: Predicting all transactions as genuine gives 99.9% accuracy
Define TP, FP, FN, TN in this context
Precision = TP/(TP+FP); recall = TP/(TP+FN)
False negatives cost money, so recall matters; F1 balances both
ROC-AUC summarises ranking across thresholds
Choose threshold from the cost of FP versus FN

bank.q: Derive the bias–variance decomposition for squared loss and use it to explain how the ridge penalty λ changes bias and variance. State how you would pick λ in practice.
outline: Model y = f(x) + ε with E[ε] = 0, Var(ε) = σ²
E[(y − f̂)²] = bias² + variance + σ²
Bias = E[f̂] − f; variance = E[(f̂ − E[f̂])²]
λ = 0 gives low bias, high variance; large λ raises bias, lowers variance
Pick λ by k-fold cross-validation on a standardised design matrix
Report the chosen λ and the validation curve

glossary.def: Predicting a numeric output from one or more inputs.
An input variable xⱼ used by the model.
The output y the model is trained to predict.
The weight w₀, the predicted value when all inputs are zero.
Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)², the quantity least squares minimises.
w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, the closed-form least-squares solution for multiple regression.
A function whose graph lies below every chord; any local minimum is global, as in least squares and logistic loss.
One full pass over the training data during gradient descent.
A small group of examples used for one gradient step, between batch and stochastic.
p/(1−p), the ratio of the probability of an event to the probability of no event.
The surface in input space where the predicted class changes, for logistic regression the line wᵀx = 0 at threshold 0.5.
The collection w = (w₀, w₁, …, w_d) of coefficients learned by a linear model.
‖w‖₂ = √(Σ wⱼ²), the quantity squared in the ridge penalty.
‖w‖₁ = Σ |wⱼ|, the quantity used in the lasso penalty.
Pulling weight estimates towards zero to reduce variance.
A setting chosen before training, such as λ or the learning rate, not learned from the gradient.
Data kept aside and used only once, to estimate final test error.
Data used to tune hyperparameters and compare models during development.
k-fold cross-validation where each fold keeps roughly the same class proportions.
TP/(TP + FP), the fraction of predicted positives that are correct.
TP/(TP + FN), the fraction of actual positives that were found.
The harmonic mean 2PR/(P + R) of precision and recall.
√((1/n) Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²), root mean squared error in the units of y.
(1/n) Σ|yᵢ − ŷᵢ|, an error measure less sensitive to outliers than RMSE.
